message.content:
Lion (family Felidae, order Carnivora) and zebra (family Equidae, order Perissodactyla) belong to two distinct mammalian lineages that split early in the evolution of placental mammals.  
Their most recent common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the clade that contains both **Carnivora** and **Perissodactyla**—the group that later gave rise to all modern odd‑toed ungulates (horses, rhinos, tapirs) and all modern carnivores (cats, dogs, bears, etc.).  

This ancestor was a small, shrew‑like insectivore that lived roughly **70 – 80 million years ago** during the late Cretaceous. It was not a lion or a zebra, but a primitive mammal that possessed the basic body plan of early placentals. From this ancestor, the lineages that would become the modern carnivores and the modern odd‑toed ungulates diverged, eventually leading to the distinct families Felidae (lions) and Equidae (zebras).
